question: What current good manufacturing practice requirements apply to the manufacturing, processing, packing, and holding of animal food?
selected_labels: FDA Guidance: Draft Guidance for Industry: Questions and Answers on the Accredited Third-Party Certification Program (draft, 2022-04-28, Docket FDA-2022-D-0370)

carve_out_sources: FDA Guidance: Draft Guidance for Industry: Questions and Answers on the Accredited Third-Party Certification Program (draft, 2022-04-28, Docket FDA-2022-D-0370)
answer:
The current good manufacturing practice requirements apply to the manufacturing, processing, packing, and holding of animal food as outlined in the FDA guidance. These requirements include:

- Preventive Controls for Animal Food (PCAF) which apply to the manufacturing, processing, packing, or holding of animal food. The scope generally applies to facilities required to register with the FDA under section 415 of the FD&C Act because they manufacture, process, pack, or hold animal food for consumption in the United States (21 CFR 507.5(a)), unless an exemption applies. [1]

- Preventive Controls for Human Food (PCHF) which apply to the manufacturing, processing, packing, or holding of human food. [2]

The guidance also specifies that for facilities manufacturing, processing, packing, or holding animal food, the CGMP regulations in 21 CFR part 507, subpart B, and the hazard analysis and risk-based preventive controls regulations in 21 CFR part 507, subpart C apply. [1]

question: What requirements apply to medicated feed manufacturing and to veterinary feed directive drugs?
selected_labels: FDA Guidance: CVM GFI #120 Veterinary Feed Directive Regulation Questions and Answers (final, 2024-04-29, Docket FDA-2010-N-0155)
FDA Guidance: CVM GFI #120 Veterinary Feed Directive Regulation Questions and Answers (final, 2024-04-29, Docket FDA-2010-N-0155)
FDA Guidance: CVM GFI #120 Veterinary Feed Directive Regulation Questions and Answers (final, 2024-04-29, Docket FDA-2010-N-0155)
carve_out_sources: FDA Guidance: CVM GFI #120 Veterinary Feed Directive Regulation Questions and Answers (final, 2024-04-29, Docket FDA-2010-N-0155)
answer: The requirements for medicated feed manufacturing include a medicated feed mill license if the VFD drug used to manufacture a Type B or Type C medicated feed is a Category II, Type A medicated article (21 CFR 558.4(a)). A list of Category II drugs is provided in 21 CFR 558.4(d). A license is not required if the VFD drug used to manufacture a Type B or Type C medicated feed is a Category I, Type A medicated article, with the exception of certain liquid and free-choice medicated feeds. If you are a university researcher and want to perform research on a drug in medicated feed, you do not need a VFD to obtain the medicated feed. The VFD regulations apply to the use of VFD drugs and VFD feed for approved, conditionally approved, and indexed indications. When investigating a new indication during the approval process or performing tests in vitro or in animals used only for laboratory research purposes, the VFD regulations do not apply. Instead, the requirements in 21 CFR part 511 “New Animal Drugs for Investigational Use” apply. If you are shipping/distributing the VFD feed directly to the client, an acknowledgment letter alone from the dealer would not be sufficient. Instead, the dealer would also need to provide you with a copy of the VFD, and both you and your dealer are required to maintain a copy of the VFD for 2 years. The dealer must ensure that any medicated feed you distribute containing a VFD drug or combination VFD drug complies with the terms of the VFD and is manufactured and labeled in conformity with the approved, conditionally approved, or indexed conditions of use for such drug. [1]

question: What is required for a biologics license application under Part 601?
answer:
Under Part 601, a biologics license application must be approved upon examination of the product and upon a determination that the product complies with the standards established in the regulations in this chapter, including but not limited to the good manufacturing practice requirements set forth in parts 210, 211, 600, 606, and 820 of this chapter. [1]  

The application must be submitted in electronic format, with the electronic submission in a form that FDA can process, review, and archive. FDA will periodically issue guidance on how to provide the electronic submission (e.g., method of transmission, media, file formats, preparation and organization of files). [2]  

For foreign establishments and products, samples for each importation must be at least two final containers of each lot of product, obtained by the District Director of Customs and forwarded to the Director, Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research or the Director, Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. A copy of the associated documents must accompany the shipment. [3]  

A biologics license issued to a manufacturer covering all locations of manufacture shall authorize persons other than such manufacturer to conduct at places other than such locations the initial, and partial manufacturing of a product for shipment solely to such manufacturer only to the extent that the names of such persons and places are registered with the Commissioner of Food and Drugs and it is found upon application that the product is in short supply due to the peculiar growth requirements of the organism involved or to the scarcity of the animal required for manufacturing purposes. [4]  

The scope of this subpart applies to radiopharmaceuticals intended for in vivo administration for diagnostic and monitoring use. It does not apply to radiopharmaceuticals intended for therapeutic purposes. [10]  

The application must include data that assess the safety and effectiveness of the product for the claimed indications in all relevant pediatric subpopulations, and to support dosing and administration for each pediatric subpopulation for which the product is safe and effective. [7]  

FDA has made available guidance documents under § 10.115 of this chapter to help you comply with certain requirements of this part. [9]  

The application must be submitted within 60 days of the anniversary date of approval of each product under the license. [29(a)]

question: How are manufacturing changes to a licensed biological product reported?
selected_labels: FDA Guidance: Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls Changes to an Approved Application: Certain Biological Products: Guidance for Industry (final, 2021-06-21, Docket FDA-1995-D-0288)
FDA Guidance: Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls Changes to an Approved Application: Certain Biological Products: Guidance for Industry (final, 2021-06-21, Docket FDA-1995-D-0288)
answer: The FDA requires that manufacturing changes to a licensed biological product be reported in accordance with the tiered-reporting system, which is based on quality risk assessment and risk management principles. If a change is approved, it must be submitted as a PAS (major change) under 21 CFR 601.12(e). If a change is minor, the CP (change plan) may be submitted for a single or multiple related changes, covering a single or multiple BLAs (biological license applications). The CP may also enable greater predictability in the timing of implementation of CMC changes, placing the product into distribution sooner, and improving the product supply chain planning. The sources that support these requirements are [1][2].

question: What is the scope of 21 CFR Part 211 and how does it relate to Part 210?

[2] 21 CFR 211.101 [2]: Written production and control procedures shall include the following, which are designed to assure that the drug products produced have the identity, strength, quality, and purity they purport or are represented to possess.

[3] 21 CFR 211.103 [3]: Actual yields and percentages of theoretical yield shall be determined at the conclusion of each appropriate phase of manufacturing, processing, packaging, or holding of the drug product. Such calculations shall either be performed by one person and independently verified by a second person, or, if the yield is calculated by automated equipment under § 211.68, be independently verified by one person.

[4] 21 CFR 211.105(a) [4]: All compounding and storage containers, processing lines, and major equipment used during the production of a batch of a drug product shall be properly identified at all times to indicate their contents and, when necessary, the phase of processing of the batch.

Such control procedures shall include, but are not limited to, the following, where appropriate:

[6] 21 CFR 211.111 [6]: When appropriate, time limits for the completion of each phase of production shall be established to assure the quality of the drug product. [10] 21 CFR 211.125(a) [10]: Strict control shall be exercised over labeling issued for use in drug product labeling operations.

[12] 21 CFR 211.132(a) [12]: General. The Food and Drug Administration has the authority under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (the act) to establish a uniform national requirement for tamper-evident packaging of OTC drug products that will improve the security of OTC drug packaging and help assure the safety and effectiveness of OTC drug products. An OTC drug product (except a dermatological, dentifrice, insulin, or lozenge product) for retail sale that is not packaged in a tamper-resistant package or that is not properly labeled under this section is adulterated under section 501 of the act or misbranded under section 502 of the act, or both.
